vignette:
Ricardo, a 53-year-old tax consultant with a background in Latin America, found himself caught in a web of distressing memories that had begun to suffocate him after a traumatic encounter with police violence. It was a seemingly ordinary evening when he witnessed an altercation in his neighborhood. The sound of sirens and the flashing lights had brought him outside, only to see an individual on the ground, visibly injured and surrounded by officers. The image of that man’s battered face haunted Ricardo, replaying in his mind with an intensity that left him breathless. Each time he encountered those images, they seeped into his thoughts, amplifying his inner narrative that he was somehow complicit in the violence he had witnessed, reinforcing his feelings of guilt and self-blame. Every time he encountered images of violence in the news, they would reinforce a creeping sense of guilt and self-blame, leading him to believe that he was somehow complicit in the violence he had witnessed. Each triggering image seemed to echo the belief that he was to blame, solidifying his inner narrative that he would never escape the shadows of that night, making him feel even more flawed and helpless. This guilt transformed into a relentless internal narrative that told him he would never be free from the shadow of that night, whispering that he was inherently flawed and deserving of the pain he felt. Whenever he passed a newsstand or scrolled through social media, any depiction of visible injuries or reminders of victims reignited the trauma. Each encounter felt like a direct assault on his sense of safety, amplifying feelings of guilt and self-blame. He had come to see himself as somehow complicit, believing that there was something within him that had made the event happen, an intrinsic fault that marked his existence. Each time he encountered a reminder of that night, it reinforced his sense of guilt, leading him to think that he was forever marked by his failure to intervene and that he would never escape the weight of his perceived complicity.

As these thoughts took root, Ricardo began to isolate himself from friends and family, feeling increasingly set apart from others. He had once enjoyed social gatherings, but now they felt like invitations to danger. The constant perception of threat made even the most mundane situations feel like potential traps, leading him to avoid places where he might encounter reminders of his past trauma. The idea of engaging with unfamiliar places became unbearable, and he would often decline invitations, fearing he might not be able to assess potential threats. Whenever he did venture out, he found himself scanning the environment, instinctively checking behind him to see if someone was following him, as if every shadow held a threat. The world outside morphed into a minefield where he constantly needed to plan escape routes, turning every outing into a mental labyrinth of anxiety. This heightened sense of threat made even mundane sights or sounds become potential triggers, as every corner seemed filled with reminders of his past trauma, leaving him in a state of perpetual alertness. His constant perception of danger led him to believe he was marked by trauma, which only deepened his vulnerability and made every sound feel like an impending threat to his safety. That sense of threat permeated his thoughts, leading him to see danger in familiar places, where reminders of his trauma lurked in every corner, poised to trigger the pain he was desperate to avoid. The constant awareness of danger made him more sensitive to reminders of his trauma, turning simple sights or sounds into triggers that echoed his fears of being unable to protect himself. This ever-present threat began to validate his deepest fears, whispering to him that he was now inherently vulnerable and would never be able to reclaim the sense of security he once had. The belief that he was now a target made every unfamiliar noise feel like an impending danger, deepening his conviction that he was a person who could not protect himself and would always be at risk. Feeling this constant fear, he had come to accept the conclusion that he was not just a victim of circumstance, but someone forever marked by trauma, reinforcing his belief that he would never feel whole again. This pervasive sense of threat validated his deepest fears, whispering to him that his life was forever altered, and that he would never escape the shadows of that night. Feeling this constant fear, he began to accept the conclusion that he was no longer the man he used to be, someone who felt safe and secure, but rather someone marked by trauma. This hyper-vigilance only deepened his sense of isolation, reinforcing the belief that he was different, that he was marked by an experience others could not understand.

The cycle of negative appraisals further tightened its grip as Ricardo’s fears began to spiral. With every confrontation of his fears, he found that the sense of menace around him only confirmed his negative beliefs, creating an endless loop where his perceived vulnerability became a self-fulfilling prophecy. His belief that he was a target, that danger was an unavoidable part of his existence, made him hyper-aware of every unfamiliar noise or person, reinforcing the notion that he could not escape the threats around him. This internal dialogue, laden with the conviction that he was always in danger, fed into a sense of vulnerability that left him feeling like he could never truly be safe again, deepening his fears and self-doubt. He often pondered the worth of his life, questioning whether it held any value after witnessing such violence. The constant sense of threat became the most convincing proof he had that his life had changed irreparably, leading him to believe that he would never again feel safe or worthy of happiness. These thoughts were not just fleeting; they were a persistent echo, reminding him that he might never feel safe again. This internal dialogue solidified his perception that he was a target, and as a result, any unfamiliar noise or person felt like an imminent threat to his safety. The belief that he was now a target confirmed the fear that he could never be safe again, leading him to feel increasingly vulnerable and unworthy of happiness. The very act of leaving his home became a negotiation with his own mind, where each decision was overshadowed by his belief that danger lurked around every corner. It was a tormenting loop that left him feeling powerless, as if every step he took was laden with the weight of his own perceived failings.

In the quiet moments, when he was alone with his thoughts, Ricardo felt the profound loneliness set in, reinforcing the idea that he was isolated from the world. The weight of these feelings made it difficult to reach out for help or even to imagine a future where he could feel whole again. Vulnerability seemed like a luxury he could not afford. He avoided therapy sessions, thinking they would only exacerbate his feelings of worthlessness. Yet, as the days turned into months, the burden of his past loomed larger, and he was left grappling with the question of whether he could ever truly escape it. The constant threat he felt served only to confirm his negative appraisals; he began to see his life as one marked by trauma, further entrenching his belief that happiness was unattainable.

Finally, after a particularly distressing incident where he saw a news report about police violence that left him in tears, Ricardo realized he could no longer bear the weight of his pain. It was a moment of clarity, a desperate hope that maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of the darkness. He felt an overwhelming need to reclaim his life, to find a path toward healing. As he sat in the waiting room of a therapist's office, he couldn't shake the fear that perhaps it was too late for him or that opening up would only lead to more suffering. Yet, with a fragile flicker of courage, he hoped for a chance to understand himself better, to learn how to navigate a world filled with reminders of pain while rediscovering the worth he had long since lost.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not establish a causal connection where triggers lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals lead to a perceived threat.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not indicate that feelings of threat lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not illustrate that a sense of threat leads to triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

It was a seemingly ordinary evening when he witnessed an altercation in his neighborhood. The sound of sirens and the flashing lights had brought him outside, only to see an individual on the ground, visibly injured and surrounded by officers. The image of that man’s battered face haunted Ricardo, replaying in his mind with an intensity that left him breathless. Every time he encountered images of violence in the news, they would reinforce a creeping sense of guilt and self-blame, leading him to believe that he was somehow complicit in the violence he had witnessed. Each triggering image seemed to echo the belief that he was to blame, solidifying his inner narrative that he would never escape the shadows of that night, making him feel even more flawed and helpless. This guilt transformed into a relentless internal narrative that told him he would never be free from the shadow of that night, whispering that he was inherently flawed and deserving of the pain he felt. Whenever he passed a newsstand or scrolled through social media, any depiction of visible injuries or reminders of victims reignited the trauma. Each encounter felt like a direct assault on his sense of safety, amplifying feelings of guilt and self-blame. He had come to see himself as somehow complicit, believing that there was something within him that had made the event happen, an intrinsic fault that marked his existence. Each time he encountered a reminder of that night, it reinforced his sense of guilt, leading him to think that he was forever marked by his failure to intervene and that he would never escape the weight of his perceived complicity.

As these thoughts took root, Ricardo began to isolate himself from friends and family, feeling increasingly set apart from others. He had once enjoyed social gatherings, but now they felt like invitations to danger. The constant perception of threat made even the most mundane situations feel like potential traps, leading him to avoid places where he might encounter reminders of his past trauma. The idea of engaging with unfamiliar places became unbearable, and he would often decline invitations, fearing he might not be able to assess potential threats. Whenever he did venture out, he found himself scanning the environment, instinctively checking behind him to see if someone was following him, as if every shadow held a threat. Feeling this constant fear, he began to accept the conclusion that he was no longer the man he used to be, someone who felt safe and secure, but rather someone marked by trauma. This hyper-vigilance only deepened his sense of isolation, reinforcing the belief that he was different, that he was marked by an experience others could not understand.
